articles.title: London’s Prince Charles Cinema faced 21 months of uncertainty over its lease; after a public campaign, the independent film venue secured a new 25-year agreement without a break clause
articles.summary: London’s Prince Charles Cinema has secured its future after 21 months of uncertainty over its lease, signing a new 25-year agreement without a break
articles.body: London’s Prince Charles Cinema has secured its future after 21 months of uncertainty over its lease, signing a new 25-year agreement without a break clause following a public campaign that attracted more than 168,000 petition signatures. The independent cinema, located near Leicester Square in London’s West End, faced the prospect of having to leave its premises if its landlord exercised a proposed redevelopment clause. The agreement, announced on October 15, 2026, brings the dispute to an end and allows the venue to continue its distinctive programme of cult classics, repertory screenings, film marathons and special events. The cinema thanked its supporters, staff and members of the film industry, whose backing helped draw national attention to the fight to preserve the venue.Prince Charles Cinema secures a new 25-year leaseThe Prince Charles Cinema announced on October 15 that it had signed a new lease covering the next 25 years, with no break clause. The agreement ends a prolonged period of uncertainty over whether the independent venue could continue operating at its current location.The cinema, situated on Leicester Place near Leicester Square, is known for screening films from across the history of cinema, including cult favourites, older releases and specialist formats. Its programme also features all-night film marathons, sing-along screenings, quizzes and other events that distinguish it from conventional multiplexes.The cinema said the new agreement would allow it to continue operating and investing in its facilities. It thanked the 168,645 people who had signed its petition, along with its staff, media supporters and members of the international film community.Why the London cinema faced 21 months of uncertaintyThe dispute began publicly in January 2025, when the cinema raised concerns about the terms proposed for its next lease by its landlord, Zedwell LSQ Ltd, which is owned by property group Criterion Capital.The cinema said the proposed agreement included a redevelopment break clause that could have required it to leave the premises on six months’ notice if the landlord secured the necessary planning permission. It also argued that the proposed rent was substantially above market rates.The possibility of early termination created difficulties for a venue that depends on maintaining specialist screening facilities and investing in its building over time. The cinema warned that uncertainty about its future could undermine its ability to plan improvements and continue its programme.Criterion Capital rejected allegations that it had attempted to intimidate or disadvantage the cinema. The landlord maintained that a break clause was standard commercial practice and that its rental expectations reflected a fair assessment of the market.The disagreement continued as the cinema sought a new lease without the redevelopment clause that had become the central issue in the dispute.168,645 people signed the campaign to save the cinemaThe campaign to preserve the Prince Charles Cinema attracted widespread public support. Its petition had gathered 168,645 signatures by the time the new agreement was announced.The campaign drew attention to the venue’s role in London’s film culture and the difficulty of replacing a specialist cinema once it closes. Supporters argued that its programming, atmosphere and commitment to older and less widely screened films made it an important part of the capital’s cultural landscape.The cinema also received support from filmmakers, actors, writers and producers. Its management thanked the international film community for helping raise awareness of the dispute and acknowledged the staff who continued running screenings throughout the uncertainty.The public campaign did not replace negotiations between the cinema and its landlord, but it helped keep the venue’s future in the public eye.Christopher Nolan, Danny Boyle and other filmmakers backed the venueThe campaign attracted support from prominent names in the film industry, including directors Christopher Nolan, Danny Boyle, Edgar Wright and Robert Eggers, as well as actor Paul Mescal.Their backing highlighted the cinema’s standing among filmmakers and audiences who value repertory screenings and opportunities to experience films on the big screen.The Prince Charles Cinema has developed a reputation for showing films that may not be readily available in mainstream cinemas. Its programme includes classic cinema, cult productions, horror marathons and screenings in formats such as 35mm and 70mm.For supporters, the potential loss of the venue represented more than the closure of a local business. They viewed it as a threat to a distinctive part of London’s film culture.Westminster Council designated the cinema an Asset of Community ValueIn May 2025, Westminster City Council designated the Prince Charles Cinema an Asset of Community Value after a recommendation from the Soho Society.The designation recognises the building’s importance to the local community. Under England’s community-asset framework, it can provide eligible community groups with an opportunity to organise a bid if the owner decides to sell, subject to the relevant rules and timescales.The status did not itself guarantee the cinema a new lease or prevent redevelopment. However, it provided formal recognition of the venue’s cultural and community significance during the dispute.The cinema thanked the Soho Society for recommending the designation and Westminster City Council for approving it.What the new agreement means for the cinemaThe 25-year lease without a break clause gives the Prince Charles Cinema greater certainty over its long-term future at Leicester Place.The agreement removes the specific early-termination mechanism that had become the focus of the campaign. It also gives the cinema a longer period in which to plan improvements to its building and screening facilities.The venue has previously said that continued investment is essential to maintaining its audience experience and its ability to screen films in different formats, from analogue projection to digital.The new lease does not guarantee commercial success, but it provides a more stable basis for the cinema to continue its operations and develop its programme.Landlord plans hotel development on upper floorsCriterion Capital has also indicated plans to develop a hotel on the upper floors of the building. The lease agreement allows the cinema to continue operating while the landlord pursues its plans for other parts of the property.Criterion Capital chief executive Vaqas Farooq welcomed the agreement, describing it as a resolution to the dispute and a commitment that would provide security for the cinema and its audiences.Cinema owner Ben Freedman also welcomed the outcome, saying it would allow the venue to plan for the future with greater confidence.The agreement brings the public dispute to a close while leaving the cinema and landlord with their respective long-term plans for the property.Why the Prince Charles Cinema matters to London's film cultureThe Prince Charles Cinema has operated as a repertory venue since 1991 and is known for programming more than 850 films a year across its two screens. The cinema says it sells more than 250,000 tickets annually and receives no public funding.Its schedule ranges from classic films and cult favourites to specialist screenings, film marathons and audience events. This mix has helped it develop a following among cinephiles in London and international visitors.The lease agreement also comes amid broader concerns about the survival of independent cultural venues in expensive city centres, where property costs and redevelopment can place pressure on businesses that serve a specialised audience.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ainsley Earhardt and Sean Hannity celebrate upcoming wedding surrounded by family and friends at Mar-a-Lago
articles.summary: Fox News hosts Ainsley Earhardt and Sean Hannity celebrated their upcoming wedding on Friday with a gathering of family, close friends and longtime colleagues at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida.
articles.body: Fox News hosts Ainsley Earhardt and Sean Hannity celebrated their upcoming wedding on Friday with a gathering of family, close friends and longtime colleagues at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida. The pre-wedding festivities brought together loved ones from different chapters of their lives for a special evening honoring the couple. "My heart is overflowing with gratitude and joy," Earhardt said. "To celebrate this beautiful season of our lives surrounded by the people we love most is truly a dream come true. God has blessed us in more ways than we could ever imagine, and I am so thankful that He brought Sean and me together. Our families, our children and our precious friends mean the world to us and sharing this moment with them makes it even more meaningful. We are so excited for this next chapter and know that the very best is yet to come." Earhardt, co-host of the network's top-rated morning program "FOX & Friends" and Hannity, the host of FOX News Channel's "Hannity" and podcast "Hang Out with Sean Hannity," announced their engagement in December 2024 after Hannity proposed over Christmas at their home church in Florida. "Ainsley is an incredible person and I couldn't be happier or more grateful that God brought us together," Hannity said. "Faith, family and friendship are what matter most in life and having so many people we love and care about together to celebrate this moment means the world to us. We are incredibly blessed and I can't thank everyone enough for being part of such a special evening." Among those celebrating were Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott and FOX News President and Executive Editor Jay Wallace as well as Earhardt's fellow "FOX & Friends" co-hosts Steve Doocy, Lawrence Jones and Brian Kilmeade, along with numerous other Fox News personalities. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump were also in attendance, along with Eric and Lara Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his wife, Jeanette, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his wife, actress Cheryl Hines, Sen. Tim Scott, Sen. Darline Graham, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, among others. "I've had a personal relationship with President Trump for over 30 years," Hannity said. "When Ainsley and I began planning this celebration, it was important to us that he could be part of this special time in our lives. We chose to host a party at Mar-a-Lago and paid fair market value for the venue. We are grateful that he and Melania could celebrate alongside our families and friends." Other guests included longtime friends of the couple, including ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith, country music legend Lee Greenwood, podcast host Sage Steele, television personality Jillian Michaels and Steve and Andrea Wynn. Both Earhardt and Hannity have longstanding careers at Fox News. Earhardt joined in 2007 and became a co-host of "FOX & Friends" in 2016 while Hannity has been with the network since its launch in 1996. The evening reflected the importance of faith, friendship and the relationships the couple has built over the years as they look forward to exchanging vows.

articles.title: In 1995, New York built a pier using recycled plastic from milk jugs and water bottles; two years of tests found three properties remained stable, but elasticity fluctuated
articles.summary: In December 1995, New York put recycled plastic lumber made from discarded milk jugs, water bottles and detergent containers to use in a pier at West
articles.body: In December 1995, New York put recycled plastic lumber made from discarded milk jugs, water bottles and detergent containers to use in a pier at West Meadow Creek, Old Field. Two years of monitoring examined how the material's engineering properties held up in the marine environment. According to the study published in ResearchGate, titled ‘Long-term engineering properties of recycled plastic lumber used in pier construction’, its dimensional stability, compression modulus and Shore D surface hardness remained similar to or greater than their original values. However, the modulus of elasticity fell after 12 months before recovering towards its initial level during the second year. The researchers said this variability limited the material's suitability to non-load-bearing structural applications.How was recycled plastic lumber tested at the West MeadowThe research examined plastic lumber profiles incorporated into the decking of a fixed pier at the West Meadow Conservation Centre in Old Field. The structure measured 1.2 metres by 9.1 metres and was partially constructed using the recycled material. The researchers tested samples before installation and collected further samples from the completed pier for laboratory examination during the monitoring period.The study investigated dimensional stability, Shore D surface hardness, in-plane compression modulus and modulus of elasticity. These measurements allowed the researchers to compare the material's engineering properties before and after exposure to outdoor marine conditions. The pier was not heavily trafficked during the monitoring period. Passenger boat trips were most frequent between May and October, at four to six trips per week, while their frequency fell to fewer than one trip per week during autumn and winter.How did recycled plastic lumber perform after marine exposureThe results showed that not every measured property deteriorated during the monitoring period. In their abstract, Breslin and his co-authors reported that the in-plane compression modulus, dimensional stability and Shore D surface hardness of the plastic lumber removed from the pier remained similar to or greater than their values before installation. The reported in-plane compression modulus was 260 ± 30 MPa, while the Shore D surface hardness was 60 ± 2.These findings provided evidence that several important characteristics of the recycled material were retained during its use on the pier. However, the results need to be distinguished from the material's performance in bending, which was assessed through its modulus of elasticity. The researchers found significant changes in that property during prolonged weathering. Consequently, the study did not establish that every engineering property remained unchanged, but it documented stability in three of the measured characteristics.How did recycled plastic lumber's elasticity change after 12 monthsThe modulus of elasticity showed a different pattern from the other measured properties. According to the researchers' abstract, its reported value decreased from 1,370 Pa to 750 Pa after 12 months of weathering. The authors described this as a decrease equal to 45% of its pre-installation value. During the second year, the modulus of elasticity increased again to a value close to its initial level.The researchers highlighted the variability in this measurement when discussing the material's suitability for construction. Their abstract concluded that the high variability in the modulus of elasticity should restrict the use of plastic lumber profiles to non-load-bearing structural applications. The findings therefore identified both the properties that remained stable and a limitation relevant to the material's structural use.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Storm Boelo: Second storm to hit UK with amber warning issued for strong wind
articles.summary: An amber weather warning has been issued for much of Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and northern England, as Storm Boelo approaches.
articles.body:
A second storm in as many days is set to batter parts of the UK, as thousands of homes remain without power following powerful winds and heavy rain on Friday.

Storm Boelo is forecast to hit on Saturday, with an amber weather warning issued from 21:00 BST across much of Scotland as well as parts of Northern Ireland and northern England where gusts of up to 80mph (128km/h) could lash exposed areas.

Travel chaos, power cuts and localised flooding are all possible as the storm sweeps in on Saturday.

The warning comes just one day after Storm Austen unleashed wind gusts in excess of 75mph, resulting in toppled trees, transport disruption and thousands of power outages.

Trains cancelled and roads warnings as Scotland prepares for Storm Boelo

Storm Austen brings power cuts and travel disruption as more wind and rain forecast

Strong winds and heavy rain will persist over the weekend as Storm Boelo moves across parts of the country.

An amber weather warning for wind has been issued for across much of Scotland, excluding the Northern Isles, as well as the far north of Northern Ireland and England from 21:00 BST on Saturday to 21:00 BST on Sunday.

Wind gusts of 60-70mph are forecast, with exposed coastal areas potentially seeing speeds of up to 80mph.

The Central Lowlands could also experience periods of disruption as strong winds funnel through the region.

Travel disruption is expected - with ScotRail has confirming that some train services will be cancelled after 21:00 on Saturday - while damage caused by the winds could lead to additional power cuts.

The second bout of bad weather comes after Austen, the first named storm of the season, brought strong wind gusts to large parts of southern England and Wales throughout Friday. Bad weather disrupted travel with fallen trees blocking railway lines and roads.

In Brighton, part of the iconic West Pier - an abandoned structure that first opened in 1866 - collapsed into the sea.

The National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 60,000 properties since Storm Austen began - but more than 10,000 homes were still without power on Friday evening.

Yellow weather warnings for wind on Saturday cover Orkney, the rest of Northern Ireland and northern England.

Gusts of 55-75mph are possible in these areas, with isolated gusts potentially reaching 80mph.

While the worst of Saturday's weather is forecast to be felt in areas covered by warnings, heavy and persistent rain is expected across larger parts of the UK.

Spray and surface water could make driving conditions hazardous, while further downpours increase the risk of localised flooding.

Strong winds are forecast to continue into Sunday, although rain should gradually ease across most of the country.

Sunny spells and blustery showers are expected elsewhere, while north-east Scotland is likely to see the most persistent rainfall.

Stormy weather to continue early next week

Once the weekend's stormy weather has passed, forecasts suggest another area of low pressure will develop over the Atlantic before deepening as it approaches the UK from the south-west.

This could bring a further spell of wet and potentially very windy weather to much of the country on Monday and into Tuesday.

Whether the system will be strong enough to be named remains uncertain.

Later in the week, high pressure is expected to build over the near continent, bringing a return to drier, calmer and more settled conditions.

Part of Brighton's iconic West Pier collapses

BBC presenter battles strong winds as Storm Austen hits Newquay

It is not unusual for storms to arrive one after another – in fact, they often develop in clusters, particularly during periods of unsettled weather across the Atlantic.

A strong jet stream is needed to help rapidly develop powerful windstorms. The process involves warmer air being pushed northwards and colder air moving southwards across large areas of the Atlantic, creating a sharp contrast in temperatures.

These temperature differences provide favourable conditions for new low-pressure systems to form and strengthen.

If these systems are then steered beneath a developing, powerful jet stream, they can intensify rapidly, potentially becoming named storms capable of bringing damaging winds, heavy rain and widespread disruption as they move towards the UK.

articles.title: Rubio floats CIA ‘partnership’ to Cubans tired of ‘failed promises, corruption’
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered Cubans a discreet CIA partnership opportunity in a Friday social media post, saying “now is the time” for those looking to “create positive change” in the Caribbean country. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered Cubans a discreet CIA partnership opportunity in a Friday social media post, saying “now is the time” for those looking to “create positive change” in the Caribbean country.

“The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said in a post to the social platform X.

The U.S. government has offered CIA partnerships to residents of adversarial countries in the past, namely in Russia — where the agency launched a Telegram campaign in 2023 to encourage intelligence sharing.

Rubio’s post came after Trump again suggested the U.S. could take military action in Cuba at a rally in Fort Myers, Fla.

“We’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran,” Trump said. “Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re gonna send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

The president’s rhetoric on Cuba has escalated throughout the year. In March, Trump said “Cuba is next” after the Iran war and that he would have the “honor” of taking over the country.

The island nation has struggled with blackouts and supply shortages as the Trump administration has increased pressure on its communist regime through sanctions and an oil blockade . Rubio said last month that Cuba was a “failed state.”

“Well, the truth is Cuba has already fallen,” Rubio told Fox New commentator Sean Hannity.

Still, it is unclear whether Trump plans to follow up on his threats of military action against Cuba. Throughout the Iran war, the president has threatened to destroy the Islamic Republic’s energy infrastructure and once warned “a whole civilization” would die unless “something revolutionarily wonderful” happened before a time limit he set — only for the U.S. to back off before the deadline.

articles.title: Tory activist in 'contract killing broker' claim had worked for party HQ
articles.summary: Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.
articles.body:
A former Tory activist who appeared to offer to "broker" the hiring of contract killers in an undercover film report previously worked for Conservative headquarters.

Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.

It comes after Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch referred to them as "shocking allegations", adding that she did not "believe that person is a member anymore".

A Conservative spokesman said Ross's party membership had "been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation". It has reported that Ross said his words were not meant to be taken seriously.

Ross was paid to provide social media advice to the party for a brief period, the BBC has been told. He was never an employee or Conservative Campaign Headquarters pass holder.

However, he met Badenoch on several occasions as part of his role as chief executive of Turning Point UK, an offshoot of a right-wing American organisation.

Ross has also met several other right-wing politicians including the former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.

In undercover filming broadcast this week by Al Jazeera, Ross appears to offer to "broker" the services of contract killers.

The Al Jazeera report said its undercover journalist approached Ross in 2022 with a fictitious situation of a family business at risk of being taken over by a criminal gang.

Ross is alleged to have asked the undercover reporter what was needed from him, and listed violent options that could be bought including stabbing, shooting and killing.

Al Jazeera said Ross denied the finding "completely" and claimed everything he said to the reporter was not meant seriously.

Turning Point UK has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Met investigates reports of letter detailing claims about Meghan's father
articles.summary: Scotland Yard opens an inquiry after the Duchess of Sussex said she was sent a letter containing "disturbing allegations".
articles.body:
The Metropolitan Police says it is investigating reports that a letter was sent to one of its specialist units in 2018 containing allegations about Thomas Markle, the father of the Duchess of Sussex.

Meghan released a statement saying that a letter was sent to the force containing "disturbing allegations" about the behaviour of her estranged father, and subsequently shared with her.

On Friday, it was reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle, 82, were found in his former home in the Philippines. The Sun newspaper, which first carried the claims , later said that the letter made direct allegations of child sex abuse against him.

UK police are not investigating Thomas Markle, who is based in the US and strenuously denies the allegations made against him.

Meghan statement offers answers after years of questions about her relationship with father

Meghan says she was informed about 'disturbing allegations' against her father in 2018

Instead, Scotland Yard has opened an inquiry to confirm the claim that the Met's royal protection unit passed on the letter to the Duchess eight years ago.

According to the Sun, the letter was sent to a Met Police unit tasked with dealing with individuals posing a threat to Royals and politicians - the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre.

A Met spokesperson said: "We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018.

"We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this."

Thomas Markle moved to the Philippines in 2025 after a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again, after having a leg amputated during surgery in December 2025.

In her statement on Friday, Meghan said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father in 2018, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told the Sun that he had allegedly found child abuse images at his father's home in the Philippines and reported it to the police.

The Undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC that "the matter is currently being investigated" by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force in Cebu.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately told the BBC that national police had secured Thomas Markle Snr's computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination.

Investigators there are currently analysing the data to determine the full scope and extent of his alleged criminal activities, with the minister saying it would take one week to get the forensic results.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigations said it was "aware of the allegations", adding it would "provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities".

The FBI's statement continued: "We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law."

Meghan is the only child of Thomas Markle's marriage to her mother, Doria Ragland, but he has two other children - Samantha and Thomas Markle Jr - from an earlier marriage.

The relationship between Meghan and her father, a former TV lighting director, broke down in the run-up to her wedding in 2018.

At the time, Thomas Markle was found to have colluded with photographers, accepting payment to stage photographs of him preparing for the wedding.

It is understood that Meghan first learnt about the allegations against her father shortly after she married the Duke of Sussex Prince Harry.

Sources close to the Sussexes said Meghan could not speak publicly about the allegations when she first learned of them, in order to avoid jeopardising any future investigation.

Speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her, the sources said.

In her statement released on Friday, Meghan said she hoped it could be understood why she had kept her distance from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

This was "to protect them", Meghan said, adding that she had "trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families".

"I am deeply distressed", she said. "My thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed".

She described the allegations as "more sickening than one could ever imagine" and said her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children".

The BBC has contacted Thomas Markle for additional comment.

Additional reporting by Virma Simonette Rivera

articles.title: DNI warned Rubio of ‘advanced’ Iranian efforts to target US personnel, memo shows
articles.summary: Iranian plots to target and kill U.S. officials in the Middle East have “substantially increased,” according to a declassified intelligence memo dated Friday, with these efforts reportedly reaching “advanced stages.” The warning, addressed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, came days after the State Department ordered the departure…
articles.body:
Iranian plots to target and kill U.S. officials in the Middle East have “substantially increased,” according to a declassified intelligence memo dated Friday, with these efforts reportedly reaching “advanced stages.”

The warning, addressed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, came days after the State Department ordered the departure of certain nonessential U.S. personnel from Saudi Arabia as the Iran-backed Houthis ramped up attacks inside the country.

“Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel,” Clayton wrote. “The lethal plotting efforts by Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries.”

The memo was first reported on by Axios, and a U.S. official confirmed its existence to The Hill’s broadcasting partner, NewsNation. Clayton’s message to Rubio does not mention the State Department’s evacuation of some American personnel from the Middle East.

The Houthis have attacked civilian infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia, including multiple attacks on airports , which have wounded and killed civilians. Saudi officials said Wednesday its military prevented another attack on the holy city of Medina.

The strikes are part of an ongoing war between Yemen’s Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

“As the Department has repeatedly emphasized, the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly, including beyond that immediate area,” a State Department spokesperson told The Hill Wednesday when asked about the decision to pull diplomats from the region.

U.S. military action in Islamic Republic has amplified the impact of the Yemen civil war throughout the Persian Gulf, as the Iran-backed Houthis have directly attacked countries in the region since its start. Saudi Arabia, due to its partnerships with the US, has been a target of much of the Houthi offensive.

articles.title: California winery founded in 1981 faces possible liquidation after $12.7 million family feud, with bankruptcy court setting a deadline to find a buyer
articles.summary: Adelaida Vineyards, which is a winery in California established in 1981, now has an uncertain future ahead of it due to a feud among family members that
articles.body: Adelaida Vineyards, which is a winery in California established in 1981, now has an uncertain future ahead of it due to a feud among family members that cost the winery $12.7 million in a judgment and caused the winery to file for bankruptcy. The winery, which is based in Paso Robles, filed under Chapter 11 of the Bankruptcy Code in December 2024, declaring about $16 million worth of debts. A bankruptcy plan required the company to find a buyer by 15 October 2026 or risk having its assets sold off. The deadline has now passed, leaving the winery’s next steps uncertain.How a family feud led to a $12.7 million judgment against Adelaida VineyardsThe problem surrounds Matthew Van Steenwyk, who is at odds with his sister Kedrin Van Steenwyk, the CEO of Adelaida. This problem had to do with allegations of financial improprieties as well as disagreements regarding the transactions made between the winery and the oil company run by the Van Steenwyks, Applied Technologies.Matthew took the matter to court regarding the way that the family businesses were being handled. The outcome was an adverse ruling against Adelaida in the amount of $12.7 million, which added to the financial woes of the winery.Court records published by Justia confirm that a judgment of $12,705,669 was entered against Adelaida in the litigation. The winery subsequently sought bankruptcy protection as the financial consequences of the dispute threatened its continued operation.Why Adelaida Vineyards filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2024Adelaida Cellars, which operates as Adelaida Vineyards & Winery, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on 13 December 2024. The filing came after the legal dispute placed considerable pressure on the business, with the winery reporting roughly $16 million in debt.Chapter 11 allows a business to pursue a restructuring or court-supervised sale rather than immediately shutting down. For Adelaida, the proceedings also created a framework for addressing creditors’ claims and determining how the company’s assets would be handled.The San Francisco Chronicle reported that the winery’s financial position had deteriorated amid the family litigation. The bankruptcy case became a critical part of the effort to resolve its liabilities, although the proceedings also raised the possibility that the business could lose its independence or cease operating.How much Adelaida Vineyards could be worth in a sale or liquidationThe winery’s financial outlook depends partly on the value that can be recovered from its property and other assets. Bankruptcy court documents cited by the San Francisco Chronicle estimated that a sale could generate between $3.8 million and $6.7 million.By comparison, the estimated recovery through liquidation was between $1.4 million and $2.8 million. The difference illustrates why finding a buyer could offer a better financial outcome than selling the assets separately, although neither valuation guarantees the amount creditors would ultimately receive.The bankruptcy plan placed Adelaida’s assets in a liquidating trust, which is responsible for administering the assets under the court-approved process. The outcome will affect the company’s creditors and determine whether the winery’s operations and property can continue under new ownership.What happens to Adelaida Vineyards after the 15 October deadline?The bankruptcy plan set 15 October 2026 as the deadline for finding a buyer. If the winery failed to secure a purchaser, its assets could be sold off under the liquidation process. That date has passed, but the available reporting does not establish whether a sale was completed or liquidation has formally begun.Adelaida’s situation is particularly significant because the business has operated in Paso Robles since 1981. Its future now depends on developments in the bankruptcy proceedings and the handling of its assets.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Pentagon designates Confucius Institutes a national security threat
articles.summary: Pete Hegseth says the Pentagon dismantled 80 ‘propaganda cells’ operating under new names at 30 universities.
articles.body:
The United States Department of Defense has designated Confucius Institutes, Chinese-funded cultural centres on university campuses, as a threat to US national security.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the move on Friday in a video posted on social media, saying the Pentagon added the organisations to its list of institutions that threaten national security.

Washington has long accused the centres of serving as Chinese propaganda tools and has taken steps to crack down on them.

Hegseth said Confucius Institutes had operated in disguise after being restricted by Congress, calling them “sleeper organisations”.

“It turns out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students,” he said.

In the video, Hegseth said that Chinese government-backed cultural programmes had infiltrated universities and reappeared in new guises despite congressional restrictions.

Over the past two months, the Pentagon has “systematically dismantled every single one of these organisations”, he said.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment.

articles.title: Israel raids towns, detains dozens of Palestinians in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Israeli military raid targets at least 15 towns in the northern West Bank, including Nablus and Jenin.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have raided towns, detaining dozens of Palestinians, hours after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced ordering a full lockdown of the occupied West Bank following an attack in the city of Hebron that killed two Israeli soldiers.

Israeli forces raided at least 15 towns in the northern West Bank, detaining dozens of Palestinians, Al Jazeera correspondents reported on Saturday.

The military raids targeted several northern cities and towns, including Nablus, Jenin, Tubas and Qalqilya.

In Nablus, Israeli forces carried out arrests and raided Palestinian homes in the villages of Jalud and Qaryut. Arrests were also reported in Arrabeh and Burqin, near Jenin, while Israeli forces entered Tubas and the nearby town of Aqqaba.

In the southern occupied West Bank, Israeli bulldozers demolished a three-storey building in Hebron, with families given five minutes to collect their belongings. Israeli forces also ordered hundreds of Palestinian families to forcibly evacuate their homes in the Ein Deir Bahha area of Hebron and its surroundings.

Israeli troops also surrounded the home of one of the suspects in the shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers in Hebron, while carrying out raids in the city’s al-Jalda neighbourhood.

The Israeli army said late on Friday that its forces began an operation in Hebron that would last “for several days”, in addition to operations by other forces in “dozens” of areas across the West Bank.

Further east, Israeli forces entered Jericho and the nearby Aqabat Jabr refugee camp.

With the lockdown, nearly 1,000 checkpoints and gates across the West Bank will be closed, affecting millions of Palestinians.

Netanyahu gave the order on Friday, shortly after the Israeli military said it had killed two Palestinian gunmen who attacked a reserve battalion near the Israeli settlement of Telem, killing two soldiers.

Israel’s ambulance service reported that at least three Israeli soldiers were injured in addition to the two who died.

All Israeli settlements, including Telem, are illegal under international law.

The attack and clampdown came amid heightened tensions across the Palestinian territory as Israeli settlers and soldiers engage in violent pogroms . Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife as aggression has been on the rise before the coming Israeli elections on Tuesday.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir responded to the killing of the Israeli soldiers by calling for Israel to take full control of the West Bank, in which the Israeli government is encouraging the construction of numerous settlements.

Mustafa Barghouti, secretary-general of the Palestinian National Initiative political party, said incitement from far-right Israeli ministers is making the situation worse.

The closure turns every city and village into “a small prison”, with checkpoints and gates blocking healthcare, the economy and education, he told Al Jazeera. He warned that collective punishment “will lead to explosions”.

articles.title: Arrest made after fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.summary: Around 200 emergency personnel are deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
articles.body:
Police in the south German state of Bavaria have detained a suspect during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.

Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 (19:15 GMT) on Friday, and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.

Difficult terrain was hindering efforts to extinguish the blaze and it was still burning early on Saturday, police said, with some 200 emergency personnel deployed. There were no reports of injuries.

The Nazi dictator used the retreat, which lies above the town of Berchtesgaden, as a part-time seat of government and met commanders there to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941.

A criminal investigation is under way to determine whether the suspect is connected to the fire.

Hitler also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.

According to its official website , it is "also a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship".

During World War Two, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews.

articles.body: A text message sent in a hurry. A joke that lands badly in the family group. A voice note recorded while angry and regretted ten minutes later. These small slips happen all year. During Mercury retrograde, astrologers say they happen more often and cost more. Mercury, the planet of speech and messages, turns backwards on October 24 and stays retrograde until November 13. For Libra, Cancer, Taurus and Aquarius, how they speak over the next three weeks may matter as much as what they say.Why Communication Gets TrickyMercury governs how people share ideas. When it’s retrograde, astrologers link the period with misheard instructions, wrong tones and messages that reach the wrong person.This retrograde sits fully in Scorpio, a sign that reads between the lines. People become more sensitive to hidden meanings. A neutral “okay” can sound cold. A delayed reply can feel like rejection.One date needs extra care. On October 30, retrograde Mercury forms a square with Mars in Leo. Mars adds heat. Words spoken that day may be sharper than intended, and arguments can flare quickly.The mood improves around November 4, when Mercury meets the Sun. Many astrologers see that as a clearer moment for honest talks. After November 13, communication generally starts moving forward again.Libra and Cancer: Words That Carry WeightFor Libra, Scorpio falls in the second house. In Vedic astrology, this house governs speech, along with family and personal money. That makes Libra’s words especially powerful during this retrograde, for better or worse.Libras usually speak with care. They’re known for diplomacy. But under pressure, their polite tone can slip into sarcasm, especially in family money discussions. A dinner-table comment about a sibling’s spending could hurt more than Libra expects. Thinking twice before speaking, particularly on October 30, can prevent days of awkward silence.For Cancer, Scorpio rules the fifth house of children, romance and creative expression. Conversations with kids may need more patience. A teenager might misunderstand a simple instruction as criticism. A young child may suddenly bring up a worry they’d been hiding.Romantic communication can also get muddled. A partner’s playful message might be misread. Cancer feels things deeply. Before reacting, asking “what did you mean by that?” can save a lot of hurt.Taurus: Conversations With a PartnerFor Taurus, Scorpio is the seventh house of marriage and partnerships. Communication with a spouse or business partner faces the biggest test.Old disagreements may come back. A promise made months ago about a holiday, a purchase, or how chores are divided may be remembered differently by each person. Taurus tends to hold firm once they’ve taken a position. That stubbornness can turn a small misunderstanding into a long standoff.The Mercury-Mars square on October 30 touches Taurus’s fourth house of home through Mars in Leo. So tensions at home may peak that day. Keep discussions short and calm, and return to them when tempers cool; it works better than trying to settle everything at once.Aquarius: Careful in PublicFor Aquarius, Scorpio is the tenth house of career and public reputation. Workplace communication needs care. Emails to seniors, posts on professional networks and comments in meetings may be read more closely than usual.An Aquarius who likes to speak frankly might share an opinion that a manager takes the wrong way. Without context, sending a message can be confusing. Double-checking before sending, especially to large groups, is wise.Mars in Leo sits in the seventh house of partners in Aquarius. So on October 30, conflict could come from a business partner or a spouse who feels unheard. Aquarians tend to explain their logic. articles.title: Robert De Niro’s 78-acre New York estate began as an 18th-century farmhouse; a converted barn now houses a gym, pool and basketball court
articles.summary: Robert De Niro’s country estate in Gardiner, New York, occupies a stretch of the Hudson Valley where the landscape has changed considerably over the
articles.body: Robert De Niro’s country estate in Gardiner, New York, occupies a stretch of the Hudson Valley where the landscape has changed considerably over the centuries. The property, acquired through a family trust in 1997, covers 78 acres and includes a farmhouse with roots in the area’s agricultural past. What began as a rural holding has since been adapted to accommodate the needs of one of Hollywood’s best-known actors, with extensive leisure facilities and separate guest accommodation. The estate has also drawn attention for reasons beyond its size. A dispute over its assessed value brought De Niro’s property arrangements into a prolonged legal disagreement with the small town where it stands.De Niro’s Gardiner estate began as a rural property with 18th-century rootsDe Niro’s connection to Gardiner dates to the late 1990s, when Riverside Trust, a legal entity associated with his family, purchased the 78-acre estate for $1.5 million, as reported by The Telegraph. Situated in Ulster County, roughly 75 miles from Manhattan, the property offered a markedly different setting from the actor’s life in New York City.The original holding included an 18th-century farmhouse beside a river, along with outbuildings. The farmhouse was reported to have seven bedrooms, six bathrooms and seven fireplaces at the time of the purchase. The estate’s history predates its association with De Niro, although the available reporting does not establish the precise construction date of the present house or confirm that every surviving part of it belongs to the original structure.The family trust later acquired another 20 acres, expanding the grounds beyond the initial purchase. The additional land included a public road leading towards the river, according to reporting published in 2014.The farmhouse and the changes made to the estateThe house and its surrounding buildings have been adapted over the years to suit the property’s use as a private family retreat. The most substantial transformation described in published accounts involved a barn that was converted into a large recreation centre. Rather than serving its former agricultural purpose, the building became a place for exercise, entertainment and leisure.The converted barn was reported to contain a gym, a basketball court, a swimming pool, a sauna, a steam room, a games room, a boxing ring and a film studio. The boxing facilities have an obvious connection to De Niro’s career, particularly his celebrated performance as a boxer in Raging Bull. The estate also includes two guesthouses, a tennis court and a small ski slope, according to the 2014 account.Its older rural setting remains central to the estate’s identity, but the outbuildings have been put to modern uses that reflect the practical requirements of a private residence. The available sources do not provide a complete architectural record of the renovations or establish when each facility was added.A dispute over the property’s valueThe Gardiner estate became the subject of public attention in 2014 after Riverside Trust challenged the local property tax assessment. Reportedly, the town had valued the holding at $5.6 million and issued a tax bill of approximately $170,000. The trust argued that the assessment was too high, putting the property’s value at $3.7 million instead.The disagreement had financial consequences for Gardiner, a small community in Ulster County. Although the town would receive only a portion of the tax revenue, it was responsible for its legal expenses in defending the assessment. By November 2014, those costs had reportedly exceeded $100,000, with further proceedings expected to add to the bill.An independent assessor appointed by the court estimated the estate’s worth at just under $9 million at a hearing earlier that year. Gardiner nevertheless agreed to retain its original $5.6 million assessment as a compromise, but Riverside Trust declined to accept that figure and continued its challenge.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: A teenager starved to death months after being detained. Her mom’s taking police to court
articles.summary: In the 18 days Runa spent in a police cell in Japan, she wrote about how much she yearned to come home. Within months of her release, she was dead.
articles.body: In the 18 days Runa spent in a police cell in Japan, she wrote about how much she yearned to come home. The teenager missed her mother’s cooking, her hugs, and their small, ordinary rituals of life together – reading, shopping, and singing. “Please, I beg you. I want to see my mom,” she scribbled in a notepad given to her during her detention, seen by CNN. Runa’s incarceration – and death months after her release – is now the subject of a lawsuit brought by her mother against Hyogo Prefectural Police alleging unlawful arrest and detention. Proceedings opened this week in a case that’s shone a spotlight on Japan’s treatment of juvenile suspects. “I feel so sorry for Runa that I failed to protect her myself,” Runa’s mother Yoko told CNN through tears and staggered breaths, using an alias for privacy reasons. CNN has withheld Runa’s full name at her mother’s request, for the same reason. Yoko said Japanese police held the 16-year-old for 18 days last year on suspicion of an assault at the care home she runs for people with special needs. Police declined to comment or share details of the complaint, and CNN has been unable to independently verify the allegations. Yoko said her daughter simply tried to prevent an agitated resident from biting others by putting her hand around the person’s chin. Runa denied the allegation and was never charged. During her incarceration, Runa stopped eating and after her release, she was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. Her weight continued to drop, and she died five months later, weighing about 20 kilograms — the average weight of a 6-year-old girl. Her single mother is seeking 109 million yen ($700,000) in damages, alleging unlawful arrest and detention, which she said led to Runa’s death. “I want the police and prosecutors to reflect on their duty to care for people and protect citizens, and to tell the truth in court,” she said. The rules around juveniles in custody Japan has a reputation for “hostage justice,” a term referring to the detention of suspects without charge for far longer than the law in other countries would allow, often for days, if not weeks. But the country also has strict rules governing how minors should be treated during a criminal investigation. Under Japan’s Juvenile Law, minors should only be incarcerated when it’s “unavoidable.” However, defense attorney Megumi Wada said the meaning of “unavoidable” had never been clearly defined, and was open to interpretation by authorities. More than 6,000 suspects under the age of 20 were detained in 2024 – and of those, 4,000 were held for more than 15 days, according to government statistics. The decision to deny Runa access to her mother, and detain her for more than a fortnight, has baffled lawyers, raising questions about whether measures to protect minors in custody are working. Mikio Uehara, a public prosecutor turned defense attorney, said Runa’s death was “extremely tragic.” “I have strong doubts as to whether detention was truly necessary,” he added. When asked for the reasons behind Runa’s detention, the Hyogo Prefectural Police said it would not “comment on the details of individual cases.” “This matter is currently the subject of a pending lawsuit for state compensation, and the prefecture’s position will be made clear in court,” a spokesperson said. Japan’s Ministry of Justice has repeatedly rejected allegations of “hostage justice,” saying that it gives due consideration to the rights of people accused of wrongdoing. A life upended The family runs a care home in Hyogo prefecture, located in the northwest of Osaka, Japan’s second-biggest city. Growing up around people who needed extra care, Runa was a “cheerful girl” who aspired to take over the family care home one day, her mother said. “Although her life was short, only 16 years, she lived every single day without ever forgetting compassion and care for others,” said Yoko. But the arrest of Runa on June 17 last year – four months after the alleged assault – upended everything. Police detained Runa at the care home and took her away before her mother, who had rushed back to the facility upon hearing the news, had a chance to see her, Yoko recalled. For the next 18 days, Yoko was barred from visiting Runa due to a ban sought by the prosecutors – and granted by a court – over concerns that she, as the owner of the facility, could tamper with the evidence. Through Runa’s lawyer, she began to learn that her daughter wasn’t eating properly. But she was never informed of the full extent as authorities rejected her requests for Runa’s meal records, she said. The night before her release, the teenager collapsed and was rushed to the hospital, she said. The next morning, Yoko was shocked by what she saw. “She had become skin and bones and came out screaming and crying,” Yoko recalled. “Her stride was so feeble it took everything she had just to walk 10 meters, not even 5 meters,” she said, adding that they had to carry her to the car. An anxious child Apart from her scribbled notes, scant details are available about Runa’s experience in detention, according to her lawyer Yoshihiro Mukai. “When we met her, she was overwhelmed with anxiety, repeatedly asking what would become of her,” Mukai told CNN, of their meetings during her detention. Japan has facilities – known as Shonen Kanbetsu Sho – dedicated to temporarily housing juvenile suspects. But defense lawyer Wada said they were seldom used when the detention was shorter than two weeks, leaving minors to face similar conditions to their adult counterparts. It’s not clear why Runa wasn’t moved to a juvenile facility after the first two weeks in custody. Wada also raised another peculiarity in Runa’s case. “I have never seen cases where the parents couldn’t see the suspects,” she said. A separate police guideline requires investigators to do their best to accommodate juvenile suspects’ requests for the company of an appropriate adult, such as a parent, even during interrogation. But the right is not absolute, said Tomonobu Ishida, a law professor at Meiji University in Tokyo. “They are essentially internal rules or administrative guidelines for the police, and therefore do not have the legally binding force,” Ishida said. “However, even assuming that there was a genuine risk of destruction of evidence, I personally have some difficulty seeing how such a relatively long period of detention could be considered proportionate, given the relatively minor nature of the alleged conduct and the fact that she was a juvenile,” Ishida said. Calls for change After Runa’s release early last July, she became suspicious of adults, including the doctors and nurses who came to treat her, Yoko said. Yoko said they tried to feed her food that might revive her appetite – from ice cream to nuts – but “everything just passed right through her system.” Runa’s distrust in the system complicated rescue efforts as she refused to be taken to hospital. Psychiatrist Mai Uchida said it’s crucial not to mistake teenagers for a “smaller version of adults,” saying their emotional and cognitive control is still developing, which causes them to experience and process stress very differently. Runa’s death was attributed to malnutrition due to an eating disorder. Loss of appetite is common following traumatic events, she said, adding that it cannot be reversed simply by encouraging the person to eat more. “It is certainly possible that PTSD could cause functional difficulties in the (gastrointestinal) system, as well as making a difference in the appetite and causing significant amount of weight loss and that would connect to death,” said Uchida, an associate psychiatry professor at Harvard Medical School. Human rights groups have long warned of the undue stress suspects in Japan are subject to during detention, ranging from aggressive questioning tactics to the lack of access to lawyers. Some legal experts said prolonged detention occurs far too often, regardless of the suspect’s age. In 2024, about 65% of the 85,040 adults detained in Japan spent more than 15 days in police custody, according to government statistics. “I completely fail to understand how such a practice is allowed to pass, and this broader reality urgently needs reform as well,” said lawyer Uehara. Yoko hopes her bid to seek justice on her daughter’s behalf could play a role in driving change. “Winning this lawsuit would mean that, even if Runa is no longer physically here, it will serve as proof that she lived and left a legacy behind to reform this justice system.”

articles.title: France prepares for day of protest a week after nationwide riots
articles.summary: More than 70,000 police officers are to be deployed over fears protesters will defy restrictions on demonstrations.
articles.body:
France is on high alert ahead of a new day of nationwide protests on Saturday, a week after the country saw some of its worst unrest in decades.

Sweeping restrictions have been imposed on demonstrations across France but hundreds of thousands of protesters are still expected to gather in Paris and elsewhere for a second round of protests organised by students, trade unions and wider anti-government groups.

The interior ministry has said it will deploy 70,000 police officers, ramping up the security presence in French cities, after the government was accused by opposition parties of failing to foresee the scale of the unrest on 17 October.

"We will not let anything go unchallenged," said Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.

"We will be uncompromising with the vandals, with the looters, and all those who commit acts of violence," he added, explaining that separate from the planned protests, numerous calls for violence had been seen on social media from the "far left and radical extreme left".

Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.

President Emmanuel Macron met high-school students' representatives on Friday ahead of Saturday's protests, and although they said he had made clear commitments to them, they said students should "continue to mobilise".

Macron decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted to take place on Saturday, and several key cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier have gone further by announcing blanket bans on gatherings .

Official announcements appear to have done little to deter organisers, with hundreds of large and small demonstrations planned across France.

After a week in which some cities have lived under partial curfews - including areas of the capital - there is an inconsistent picture across France's cities as to what level of protest will be permitted by authorities.

While some mayors have pressed ahead with broad bans, others have agreed to allow demonstrations registered with authorities - for example, in Marseille, a previous order barring all protests was swiftly reversed to allow a trade union-organised march to go ahead.

In Paris, a march organised by the student trade union and supported by labour groups has been ordered to stick to a route which does not go through the city centre - though preparations for unrest in some of the city's most recognisable areas are under way regardless.

The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums will all be closed on Saturday, a scheduled home match for football team PSG has been moved to Monday, and some businesses have boarded up their windows in anticipation of further looting.

In a sign of how a student-led protest movement expanded to become a wider anti-government outpouring, protesters associated with a revived gilet jaunes (yellow-vest) movement could be out in force across France on Saturday.

The protest movement, which has attracted support from left and right, led huge disruptive demonstrations during Macron's first term in office.

A website associated with the group listed more than 500 planned demonstrations and some 200 other actions on Saturday, and demanded that Macron resign.

In its online call for action, the group said "we refuse to add our voices to the chorus of outrage" over the violence on 17 October and accused police of attacking protesters.

France is still reeling from last week's unrest, which saw police vastly outnumbered by protesters and rioters, shops looted and buildings torched - perhaps most emblematically, the ornate 19th-Century town hall in Limoges .

On Friday, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 232 people had been imprisoned for their role in the 17 October riots, and more than 1,100 had appeared in court. Around 260 of those cases involves "charges of organised gang activity", he added.

Darmanin has ordered prosecutors to seek punitive measures against people convicted of looting or attacking police officers, including banning them from taking part in demonstrations, removing their right to vote and barring them from accessing social media.

Disillusionment is high among the French public, who have seen cost-of-living pressures increase, and who are faced with increasingly dire warnings that any future government will likely have to make deep spending cuts in order to finance spiralling levels of debt.

On top of that, the recent unrest has played out against the backdrop of a polarised political landscape and with France preparing for what could be the most divisive and unpredictable election period in a generation.

Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest a candidate from his centrist movement could fail to make it through to a run-off vote in May between the top two contenders.

That would likely leave French voters to choose between the hard-right National Rally and radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed).

Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron and his ministers, sensing fertile ground among the French public after a period in which his centrist party has struggled to form functioning governments and pass legislation.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader and presidential candidate of La France Insoumise, has criticised what he has framed as heavy-handed policing of demonstrations and has accused Macron of "destroying the republican state" by imposing restrictions.

He has called on his supporters to join protests on Saturday as he did the previous week, before condemning the rioting which followed.

A two-day National Rally conference in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) to the south of Paris, could prove to be a flashpoint on Saturday.

Left-wing groups are expected to descend on the small city, where thousands of members of the hard-right party are set to gather to hear its leader Marine Le Pen speak.

This week, the city's mayor warned the numbers expected in Orléans were "unprecedented", and said thousands of police would be deployed to manage any clashes, adding that public transport would be suspended.

Opinion polls suggest Le Pen could have her strongest chance yet of becoming president as she runs for a fourth time, despite a court finding her guilty of embezzling EU funds earlier this year. She has denied committing any offence and is appealing the verdict.

articles.title: Festive prep up: Simple ways to clean appliances this festive season
articles.summary: Preparing your home for the festive season gives the house a bright new feel.
articles.body: Preparing your home for the festive season gives the house a bright new feel. Painting walls and clearing clutter are good first steps, but your everyday appliances carry the biggest burden during the holidays. When you bake sweets or wash loads of party laundry, a clean appliance keeps everything running smoothly. Well, we have curated a guide that may help in step‑by‑step deep cleaning for some of the most essential household appliances with kitchen items you already have.Deep‑clean the refrigerator with baking sodaClear and Sort: First unplug the fridge. Clear every shelf. Toss out condiments, old pastes and forgotten leftovers.Wipe with Soda: First mix two tablespoons of baking soda into a bowl of water. Then dip a microfiber cloth into this solution and wipe down the inner walls, vegetable trays and glass racks.Target the Seals: Take a toothbrush dip it in the same soda solution and use it to clear dust or sticky residue that is trapped inside the rubber door gaskets.Baking soda naturally neutralises food smells and does not leave harsh chemical scents that can stick to uncooked food.Refresh the microwave using lemon steamPrepare the Bowl: Fill a microwave‑safe bowl with one cup of water then squeeze the juice of one lemon into it. Drop the lemon halves into the water.Steam It Out: Heat the bowl on power for three to five minutes until the water boils and the glass door fogs up with steam.Rest and Wipe: Keep the door closed for another five minutes so the acidic steam can soften baked‑on grease. Then remove the bowl carefully. Wipe the interior walls and turntable with a dry towel.Degrease the kitchen chimney and gas stoveSoak Chimney Filters: detach the baffle or mesh filters from your kitchen chimney. Next submerge them in a bucket of boiling water that contains a squirt of dishwashing liquid and half a cup of washing soda or vinegar. Let the filters soak for twenty to thirty minutes.Scrub the Stove: While the filters soak spray a mixture of water and liquid detergent, over the gas stove top. Then use a non‑abrasive sponge to lift dried curry drips and oil rings.Clear Burner Ports: Clear the brass burner holes with a safety pin or thin wire so that gas flows evenly and the flame remains a blue.Descale and sanitize the washing machineWith lots of silk sarees, thick curtains and everyday festival clothes piling up your washing machine works hard during the holidays. Hard water deposits and leftover detergent can make clothes smell bad.Run a Vinegar Cycle: Pour two cups of distilled vinegar directly into the drum or liquid detergent dispenser. Run a cycle on the highest temperature setting to break down limescale deposits and soap scum.Clean the Trap: Open the drain filter access panel drain any leftover water into a tray and wash out lint or debris trapped inside the filter under running tap water.Aerate the Drum: Wipe down the rubber door seal to prevent mold growth and leave the door open for an hour so the drum dries completely.De-odorize the dishwasher with vinegar and baking sodaIf you depend on a dishwasher to handle stacks of serving bowls and dinner plates during family gatherings, getting it ready beforehand saves time later.Clear the Filter: Twist out the drain filter rinse away trapped food scraps under warm water and put it back in place.Dissolve Built-Up Grease: Place a glass bowl filled with one cup of vinegar on the top rack of an empty machine. Run a hot water cycle to dissolve grease and mineral buildup.Polish and Deodorize: Sprinkle half a cup of baking soda across the tub floor and run a short hot rinse.
